title: Review: telling your week
why: This review brings together everything from unit 2: telling the time, days and dates, pronominal verbs, adjectives and the three regular verb groups. You put it all to work describing a real week, with a schedule and a grocery bill, before moving on to the big irregular verbs of unit 3.

{"lessons": ["

A week in French

This lesson adds nothing new: it brings together everything from unit 2 so you can tell someone about your week, hour by hour and day by day. Let's start with the frame: days, times and the moments of the day.

Lundi or le lundi?

Days of the week are lowercase in French, like months: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. Without an article, a day means the next one coming, this week: Lundi, je travaille tard (this Monday, I'm working late). With le, it means every week: Le lundi, je travaille tard (on Mondays, I work late). English adds an -s to the day; French adds le and keeps the day singular.

Le samedi, je me lève tard. Mais samedi, je travaille.On Saturdays I get up late. But this Saturday I'm working.

Moments of the day

No preposition is needed for “in the morning” or “in the evening”: French simply uses the article. For a precise time, “at” is always à.

FrenchEnglish
le matinin the morning
l'après-midiin the afternoon
le soirin the evening
à sept heures et demieat half past seven
à midi / à minuitat noon / at midnight
à 18 h 15 (dix-huit heures quinze)at 6:15 p.m.

Midi and minuit never take heures: à midi, not “à midi heures”.

For schedules (trains, shops, classes, appointments) French uses the 24-hour clock: Le cours finit à 20 h 30, read vingt heures trente. In conversation, people also say huit heures et demie du soir.

", "

Your day: the three verb groups

A typical day in French is full of pronominal verbs. The little pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) always matches the subject, and it becomes m', t', s' before a vowel.

Je me réveille à six heures et demie, je me lève, je me douche et je m'habille.I wake up at half past six, I get up, I shower and I get dressed.

In the negative, ne… pas wraps the pronoun and the verb together: the pronoun stays glued to its verb.

Le dimanche, je ne me lève pas tôt.On Sundays, I don't get up early.

And here are the three regular groups side by side. Same subjects, three sets of endings:

parlerfinirattendre
je (j')parlefinisattends
tuparlesfinisattends
il, elle, onparlefinitattend
nousparlonsfinissonsattendons
vousparlezfinissezattendez
ils, ellesparlentfinissentattendent
  • The -ent of ils parlent is silent: il parle and ils parlent sound the same.
  • Finir adds -iss- in the plural, and you can hear it: il finit / ils finissent.
  • Il attend has no ending and its d is silent; in ils attendent the d becomes audible.

“To wait for” is just attendre, with no preposition: J'attends le bus, Nous attendons Léa. But “to answer someone” needs à: Elle répond à Hugo.

", "

Numbers, prices and descriptions

A week also means shopping. Here's a receipt from a Saturday morning in Toulouse. Read each price aloud before you look at the right-hand column.

ItemPriceRead aloud
une baguette1,10 €un euro dix
un poulet11,90 €onze euros quatre-vingt-dix
des pommes4,35 €quatre euros trente-cinq
un fromage7,80 €sept euros quatre-vingts
des yaourts3,25 €trois euros vingt-cinq
un gâteau14,50 €quatorze euros cinquante
Total42,90 €quarante-deux euros quatre-vingt-dix

Remember the comma: 4,35 € is a French price, and you say the euros first: quatre euros trente-cinq. To ask for the total: Ça fait combien ? or C'est combien ? Watch out for 70 to 99: soixante-dix (60 + 10), quatre-vingts (4 × 20, with an -s), quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10), and no -s as soon as another number follows: quatre-vingt-cinq.

Describing your flat and your week

Adjectives agree with the noun and usually come after it, but a short group (beau, joli, bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, nouveau…) comes before.

L'appartement est petit, mais la cuisine est grande et très lumineuse.The apartment is small, but the kitchen is big and very bright.
C'est une semaine chargée : j'ai un nouveau travail !It's a busy week: I have a new job!

Très goes with adjectives (très chargée), beaucoup with verbs (Je travaille beaucoup) and beaucoup de with nouns (beaucoup de cours). Never “très beaucoup”.
